title: The equals() and hashCode() Contract in Sets
summary: Why breaking the equals/hashCode contract causes elements to vanish inside HashSets, causing duplicate insertions and phantom data.
prerequisites: HashSet: How Hash Buckets Guarantee O(1) Lookups
learningObjectives: Deeply understand the mathematical invariants of the equals() and hashCode() contract
Diagnose the silent 'vanishing element' bug caused by mutating objects stored in a HashSet
Analyze bucket recalculation mismatch when object hash codes change dynamically
Design bulletproof, immutable domain value objects for safe Set storage
expectedOutcomes: Ability to prevent and debug subtle memory leaks and corrupted collections in production code
Mastery of equals() and hashCode() generation conforming strictly to Joshua Bloch's Effective Java rules

activities.title: Practical Context: Moving Locker Keys in a High-Security Facility

analogy.headline: Practical Context: Moving Locker Keys in a High-Security Facility
analogy.story:
Imagine a bank vault with 1,000 safety deposit boxes. A customer arrives with their passport ID, the teller computes a locker number from the passport number, and places their valuables in Box #42.

Later, the customer legally alters their passport ID without telling the bank. When they return, the teller takes the new passport, computes a new locker number (Box #89), and opens it: Box #89 is completely empty! The customer panics and claims their valuables were stolen, but the items are still sitting undisturbed in Box #42, now permanently inaccessible.

This is precisely what happens when an object field is mutated after insertion into a HashSet.
analogy.keyTakeaway: Mutating fields used in hashCode() after set insertion changes the object's bucket address. The set looks in the new bucket, fails to find it, and reports the object does not exist.

activities.title: The equals() and hashCode() Contract: The Vanishing Element Disaster

keyTakeaways: If two objects are equal according to equals(), their hashCode() methods MUST return the same integer
If two objects have the same hashCode(), they are NOT necessarily equal (hash collision)
Mutating an object after inserting it into a HashSet changes its hash code, stranding it in the wrong bucket
Always make objects stored in Sets immutable (using final fields or Java records)

activities.title: Fixing Corrupted Sets with Immutable Records
activities.description: Transform a broken mutable set design into a resilient, production-ready architecture using Java records.

steps.description: Declare an immutable Java record. The compiler automatically generates consistent, final equals() and hashCode() methods.
Insert the immutable key into a HashSet. The hash code is mathematically invariant across the lifetime of the application.
Verify set contains the key reliably, eliminating any possibility of hash corruption or vanishing elements.

questions.question: What happens if a class overrides equals() but fails to override hashCode() when used in a HashSet?
options: Identical objects will produce different memory-address hash codes, causing duplicate entries in the HashSet
The HashSet automatically synthesizes a hashCode()
An UnsupportedOperationException is thrown at runtime
questions.explanation: If hashCode() is omitted, Object.hashCode() uses identity hashing. Two logically equal objects will produce different hash codes, land in different buckets, and both be added, violating Set uniqueness.

questions.question: Why does set.contains(obj) return false after obj has a field mutated, even though obj is still inside the set?
options: Because HashSet clears all elements whenever any object is modified
Because the set recalculates the bucket index using the mutated hash code, searching a bucket different from where the object was originally stored
Because the Garbage Collector automatically deletes mutated objects
Because Java detects mutations and marks the object as invalid
questions.explanation: HashSet finds elements by computing (capacity - 1) & hash(key). If key.hashCode() changed, the set searches the wrong bucket and fails to locate the object.

questions.question: Which fields should be included in an object's hashCode() calculation?
options: All fields declared in the class, including transient and static variables
Only the exact same fields that are compared in the equals() method
A random integer generated in the constructor
questions.explanation: To maintain the equals/hashCode contract, hashCode() must use the exact same fields as equals(). If equals() uses id and name, hashCode() must use id and name.

questions.question: What is the best architectural practice when storing domain objects in a Set?
options: Use reflection to update hash codes before querying
Design Set elements as immutable objects (e.g. Java records) or base equals/hashCode solely on an immutable unique identifier
Call set.clear() and re-add all elements before any contains() check
Avoid Sets and use primitive arrays exclusively
questions.explanation: Immutability guarantees that hash codes never drift, completely preventing vanishing element bugs and memory leaks.

activities.title: Technical Interview: Hash Invariants & Bug Post-Mortems

questions.question: Walk me through how you would debug a production bug where a HashSet contains 10,000 elements, but set.contains(myObject) returns false despite myObject being in the set.
questions.answer: This is the classic mutable hash corruption bug. First, I would inspect the class definition of myObject to see if equals() and hashCode() depend on mutable fields (e.g. status, timestamp, balance). Next, I would check if any thread modified those fields after insertion. If the field changed, its hashCode() changed, stranding the object in an orphaned bucket. To confirm, I would iterate over the set manually with a for-each loop: `for (var item : set) if (item.equals(myObject)) found = true;`. If the linear loop finds it but set.contains() returns false, hash code drift is 100% verified. The fix is to make the key immutable or base hashing strictly on an immutable ID.

questions.question: Why does HashMap / HashSet use prime multiplier 31 in hashCode generation?
questions.answer: Joshua Bloch explains in Effective Java that 31 has two key properties: 1) It is an odd prime. If an even number like 2 or 4 were used, multiplication would equate to bit shifting, discarding high-order information and increasing collisions. 2) Modern JVM JIT compilers automatically optimize `31 * i` into `(i << 5) - i` (a single shift and subtract instruction), executing much faster than a standard multiplication.

questions.question: Can you have a memory leak in Java caused by a HashSet?
questions.answer: Yes, and it is common. If mutable objects are added to a HashSet and their fields mutate, calling `set.remove(object)` will fail because the set checks the wrong bucket. As a result, the object can NEVER be removed through normal set operations. Furthermore, the internal HashMap retains strong references to the object indefinitely, preventing the Garbage Collector from freeing it, resulting in a persistent heap memory leak.

practiceProblems.title: Diagnose Vanishing Element
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Given a set containing an account whose balance was mutated, implement recoverVanishingElement(Set<Account> set, String targetId) that finds and returns the account by linear scan since set.contains() fails.

testCases.input: set containing mutated account with targetId = 'ACC-1'

hints: A for-each loop iterates through all buckets directly without recalculating hashes.

practiceProblems.title: Implement Bulletproof Immutable Set Element
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Define an immutable record UserCredential(String username, String domain) with validation that throws IllegalArgumentException if either field is null or blank.
hints: Use compact constructor syntax for records: public UserCredential { ... }.

practiceProblems.title: Fix Broken equals() Without hashCode()
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Fix the Product class so that two products with identical sku codes are recognized as equal and produce identical hash codes.

testCases.input: Product p1 = new Product('A', 'Name1'); Product p2 = new Product('A', 'Name2');

hints: Because equals() compares only 'sku', hashCode() must also hash only 'sku'.

practiceProblems.title: Calculate Stable Hash Code
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Implement a method computeHash(String id, int version) that uses the formula: 31 * id.hashCode() + version.
hints: Handle id == null safely by treating its hash as 0.

practiceProblems.title: Clean Corrupted Set Entries
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Given a HashSet that may contain duplicate elements due to broken hash codes, reconstruct a clean HashSet<Product> where every element is verified distinct using its sku.

testCases.input: Set with 3 items where 2 share the same SKU

hints: Iterate over the dirty set linearly.
Index products into a Map<String, Product> by SKU using putIfAbsent.
